sentence: If symptoms are affecting studies, work or relationships, the NHS advises making a GP appointment.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes the diagnostic criteria as symptoms that have been present since childhood, persist, and cause at least moderate impairment across two or more areas of life: home, work, education and relationships.

A large proportion of adults with ADHD have another condition too, such as anxiety, depression, autism, a tic condition such as Tourette syndrome, substance use, or physical health problems including chronic pain and fatigue.
There is no single test for ADHD.
For children, NICE says primary care practitioners should not make the initial diagnosis or start medication.
If problems persist with at least moderate impairment, they refer to secondary care, such as a child psychiatrist, a paediatrician or a specialist ADHD child and adolescent mental health service.
NICE says the diagnosis must be made by a specialist psychiatrist, paediatrician or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional.
For adults, the GP asks about the symptoms and how they affect life, and may consider other conditions that could be causing them, such as autism, Tourette's syndrome or anxiety.
A specialist assessment asks about the history of symptoms, particularly whether they started in childhood and how they affected school.
An adult diagnosis cannot be confirmed unless symptoms have been present since childhood.
NICE says a diagnosis should not be made solely on the basis of rating scale or observational data, although rating scales are helpful added tools.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists likewise says an ADHD diagnosis should never be based solely on questionnaires.
NICE also says clinicians should discuss the positive and negative impacts of receiving a diagnosis, such as stigma and labelling.

The NHS says ADHD in adults is managed through lifestyle changes, workplace adjustments or medicines, and talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) or mindfulness may be recommended.
ADHD medicines must be started and monitored by an ADHD specialist.
The GP may later take over prescribing under a shared care agreement, although this is the GP's decision and not every practice does it.
NICE advises local protocols for shared care with primary care and a written treatment plan shared with the person with ADHD.
NICE notes that for some people symptoms and impairment may be reduced through environmental modifications, such as a modified school curriculum or choice of employment.
The guideline asks for modifications to be checked before medication starts.

A European consensus statement on adult ADHD advises multimodal treatment made up of psychoeducation, pharmacotherapy, coaching and/or CBT, ideally involving the person's partner, family or close friends.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists says early years support and reasonable adjustments at school and work can help reduce the impact that ADHD has on people's lives.
ADHD affects people in different ways, and the Royal College of Psychiatrists' information for adults covers both the challenges and the strengths people with ADHD can have.

A 2023 thematic analysis of adults' positive experiences found that being creative, having novel ideas, seeing things from a different perspective and being good at finding solutions were commonly described as strengths.
A MedlinePlus support guide describes ADHD as a lifelong journey and says understanding and acceptance from others can make a world of difference.
ADHD UK provides information and support for anyone affected by ADHD, including a self-screening tool and support groups.
Waiting times for specialist adult ADHD services vary, and in some areas it can take several months or years to be seen.
